nodes.name: Ebenezer Scrooge

nodes.name: Ghost of Christmas Past
nodes.description: Ghost of Christmas Past is a phantom that shows things past. | The Ghost of Christmas Past is a spirit that appears to Scrooge, with a fluctuating and indistinct form, and speaks softly about Scrooge's past. | The Ghost of Christmas Past is a spirit that shows Scrooge scenes from his past, including the Fezziwig party. | The Ghost of Christmas Past is a supernatural being who shows Scrooge visions of his past, characterized by a sense of urgency as time grows short. | The Ghost of Christmas Past is a spectral figure that previously showed Scrooge visions from his past, as recalled during the music at the gathering.

nodes.name: Ghost of Christmas Present
nodes.description: Ghost of Christmas Present is a spirit of a kind, generous, and hearty nature. | A spirit of a kind, generous, and hearty nature. | The Ghost of Christmas Present is a jolly spirit dressed in a green robe with white fur, barefoot, wearing a holly wreath, and carrying a torch. nodes.name: Mr. Topper

nodes.name: Dick Wilkins

nodes.name: Martha Cratchit

nodes.name: Fred
nodes.description: Fred is Scrooge's nephew, whom Scrooge asks for entry to dinner. | Fred is Scrooge's nephew, who, despite pity for his uncle, maintains good humor and intends to visit Scrooge every year to wish him well. | Fred is Scrooge's nephew who instigates the guessing game and proposes a toast to Uncle Scrooge. | Fred is Scrooge's nephew, who welcomes Scrooge into his home for dinner. | Fred is a character who comes to dinner and is warmly welcomed, indicating a positive relationship with the host.

nodes.name: Counting-house

nodes.name: Fog
nodes.description: The fog is a dense, cold atmospheric condition that pervades the environment outside and seeps into the counting-house.

nodes.name: Fire
nodes.description: There are small fires in the counting-house; Scrooge's fire is small, and the clerk's fire is even smaller, consisting of one coal.

nodes.description: The coal-box is kept in Scrooge's room, preventing the clerk from replenishing his fire.

nodes.description: The candle is used by the clerk in an attempt to warm himself, though he fails due to lack of imagination.

nodes.name: Scrooge's Clerk

nodes.name: The Ghost
nodes.description: The Ghost is a supernatural apparition that confronts Scrooge about his beliefs and demonstrates its reality through frightful actions. | The Ghost is the spectral form of Jacob Marley who visits Scrooge to warn him about the fate that awaits him if he does not change his ways. | The supernatural entity that appears to Scrooge, identified as the ghost of Jacob Marley, bound in chains and expressing regret for his past life. | The Ghost is a spectre that listens to the phantoms' lamentations and joins in their mournful dirge before floating out into the night. | The Ghost is a supernatural being that appears as a child-like figure with white hair, long muscular arms, a tunic of purest white, a lustrous belt, and a jet of light from its head. It holds a branch of fresh green holly. | The Ghost is a spirit who guides Scrooge through recollections of his past, pointing out significant scenes. | The Ghost is a supernatural being that Scrooge observes and communicates with during the narrative. | The Ghost is a spirit that accompanies Scrooge, showing him scenes from his past and questioning the significance of Fezziwig's actions. | A supernatural entity that forces Scrooge to observe scenes from the past. | The Ghost is a supernatural spirit whose light is bright and which Scrooge attempts to extinguish. | The Ghost is a supernatural character who instructs Scrooge to touch its robe, leading to a transformation of the scene. | The Ghost is a spirit that shows Scrooge the Cratchit family and reveals the potential future of Tiny Tim. | The Ghost is a supernatural being who rebukes Scrooge and guides him to observe the Cratchit family. | The Ghost is a supernatural entity that accompanies Scrooge and observes the party with him. | The Ghost (likely the Ghost of Christmas Present) is a supernatural entity that shows Scrooge scenes of various homes and refuges. | The Ghost, likely the Ghost of Christmas Present, appears to age during the night and reveals two children hidden beneath its robe. | The Ghost is a supernatural being guiding Scrooge, pointing to a head and revealing a scene of a family. | The Ghost is a supernatural entity that guides Scrooge through various scenes. | The Ghost is a spectral entity that shows Scrooge visions, including his neglected grave, and remains immovable until Scrooge's entreaties.

nodes.name: Mankind's Welfare
nodes.description: The ideal that charity, mercy, forbearance, and benevolence should be one's primary business, as emphasized by the ghost.

nodes.name: Christian Spirit
nodes.description: The notion of a spirit working kindly in its sphere, serving as a moral ideal for mortals.

nodes.name: The Three Spirits
nodes.description: The Three Spirits are supernatural beings that will visit Scrooge to give him a chance to escape Marley's fate.

nodes.name: The Phantoms
nodes.description: The phantoms are wandering spirits in the air, each wearing chains like Marley's Ghost, and they express sorrow and regret over lost opportunities to do good.

nodes.name: The Old Ghost in a White Waistcoat
nodes.description: This ghost is an elderly spirit, recognizable to Scrooge, who is burdened by an iron safe and cries at his inability to help a woman and infant on a doorstep.
nodes.id: The Old Ghost in a White Waistcoat

nodes.name: The Invisible World
nodes.description: The Invisible World represents the supernatural realm that Scrooge glimpses, which contributes to his emotional state and need for rest.

nodes.name: The Church Bell
nodes.description: The church bell is the clock in the neighboring church that strikes the quarters and then rings up to twelve, marking the time for Scrooge.

nodes.name: Scrooge's Repeater
nodes.description: Scrooge's repeater is a pocket watch that he uses to check the time, but it also strikes twelve, adding to his confusion about the actual time.

nodes.name: The Clock
nodes.description: The heavy bell and clock in Scrooge's residence ring from six to twelve and then stop, leading Scrooge to suspect an icicle interfering with the works.

nodes.name: The First of Exchange
nodes.description: A financial document mentioning Mr. Ebenezer Scrooge, referenced in the text as part of Scrooge's thoughts about counting days.

nodes.name: The Visitation
nodes.description: The predicted supernatural visitation that Marley's Ghost warned Scrooge about, expected when the bell tolls one.

nodes.name: The Hour Bell
nodes.description: The hour bell is a bell that chimes the hours and signals the arrival of the supernatural visitor.

nodes.name: Spirit
nodes.description: The Spirit is a supernatural entity that leads Scrooge through time, taking him to a past winter day on an open country road. | A supernatural being that carries a torch and sprinkles drops on dinners, engaging in dialogue with Scrooge. | The Spirit is another supernatural entity that stands by Scrooge and looks approvingly at the nephew. | The Spirit is a supernatural figure standing by Scrooge's side, observing the scene with approving affability. | A phantom ghost that guides the protagonist through the future, observing conversations and scenes.

nodes.name: Country Road
nodes.description: A country road with fields on either hand, representing the rural area where Scrooge grew up, now covered in snow.

nodes.name: Market Town
nodes.description: A small market-town in the distance with a bridge, church, and winding river, associated with Scrooge's childhood memories.

nodes.name: Boys
nodes.description: Boys riding shaggy ponies or in gigs and carts, depicted as joyful and full of spirits, calling to each other and exchanging Christmas greetings.

nodes.name: Farmers
nodes.description: Farmers who drive the country gigs and carts, part of the scene of Scrooge's past.

nodes.name: The School
nodes.description: The School is a neglected building in Scrooge's past, where he was left alone during Christmas as a child.

nodes.name: Ali Baba
nodes.description: Ali Baba is a fictional character from a story, who appears as a vision to Scrooge, representing a source of comfort and imagination for his younger self. | A character from the story of Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves, seen by Scrooge as a figure from his past, appearing with an axe and an ass laden with wood.

nodes.name: The Boy (Scrooge as a child)
nodes.description: The Boy is a young Scrooge, left alone at school, neglected by friends, and reading near a fire.

nodes.name: Valentine
nodes.description: A character from a story, referred to as Valentine, with a wild brother named Orson.

nodes.name: Orson
nodes.description: The wild brother of Valentine in a story, mentioned by Scrooge.

nodes.name: Sultan's Groom
nodes.description: A character who was turned upside down by the Genii, mentioned by Scrooge.

nodes.name: Genii
nodes.description: Mythical beings who turned the Sultan's Groom upside down.

nodes.name: Princess
nodes.description: The Princess to whom the Sultan's Groom was married, as mentioned by Scrooge.

nodes.name: Parrot
nodes.description: A parrot with a green body and yellow tail that Scrooge recalls from a story, associated with Robin Crusoe.

nodes.name: Robin Crusoe
nodes.description: A character from the story of Robinson Crusoe, who kept a parrot named 'Poor Robin Crusoe'.

nodes.name: Friday
nodes.description: A character from the story of Robinson Crusoe, running for his life to a creek.

nodes.name: The Spirit
nodes.description: The Ghost of Christmas Past, who is showing Scrooge visions of his past Christmases. | The Spirit is a supernatural being, likely the Ghost of Christmas Present, who engages in dialogue with Scrooge and demonstrates the ability to fit into any space. | The Spirit is a supernatural entity accompanying Scrooge, exulting in the warmth and gatherings of the homes they pass. | The Spirit, also known as the Ghost of Christmas Present, shows Scrooge the children Ignorance and Want, and warns about the boy Ignorance. | The Spirit is a phantom-like entity that guides Scrooge through various scenes, pointing out meetings and conversations.

nodes.name: The Boy Singing Carol
nodes.description: A boy who was singing a Christmas carol at Scrooge's door the previous night, mentioned by Scrooge.

nodes.name: The Schoolmaster
nodes.description: The Schoolmaster is a person at the school who announces Scrooge's box, glares at him, and hosts a farewell gathering with wine and cake.

nodes.name: Scrooge's Box
nodes.description: Scrooge's Box is a container that is brought down at the school and likely holds Scrooge's belongings for his departure.

nodes.name: School Setting
nodes.description: The school is the location where Scrooge is staying and is visited by Fan; it is also where the schoolmaster appears.

nodes.name: The Parlour
nodes.description: The parlour is a cold room in the school where the schoolmaster entertains the children with wine and cake.

nodes.name: Master Scrooge
nodes.description: Master Scrooge is a young boy who is a student at the school and is leaving it in a chaise.

nodes.name: Schoolmaster
nodes.description: The schoolmaster is the person who produces the wine and cake and bids the children goodbye.

nodes.name: Ghost
nodes.description: The Ghost is a supernatural being that accompanies Scrooge and shows him scenes from his past, including his time at school and his apprenticeship at Fezziwig's warehouse. | The Ghost is a supernatural being showing Scrooge shadows of the past, embodying various faces. | The Ghost is a supernatural being that travels with Scrooge, showing him various scenes, including a miner's hut and the sea. | The Ghost is a spectral entity that leads Scrooge on a journey across time and space, showing him scenes of Christmas in various locations.

nodes.name: Old Fezziwig
nodes.description: Old Fezziwig is a cheerful gentleman who runs a warehouse where Scrooge was apprenticed. | Old Fezziwig is a host of a festive dance event, leading the dancing and interacting with guests, showing energetic and joyful behavior.

nodes.name: Postboy
nodes.description: The postboy is a servant who is offered a glass of 'something' by the schoolmaster's servant but declines.

nodes.name: Decanter of Light Wine
nodes.description: A decanter containing curiously light wine, produced by the schoolmaster.

nodes.name: Block of Heavy Cake
nodes.description: A block of curiously heavy cake, produced by the schoolmaster.

nodes.name: Warehouse
nodes.description: The warehouse where Scrooge was apprenticed to Fezziwig. | The warehouse is Fezziwig's place of business that is transformed into a ballroom for the Christmas Eve party.

nodes.name: School
nodes.description: The school from which Master Scrooge departs at the beginning of the scene.

nodes.name: Fezziwig
nodes.description: Fezziwig is a jovial and energetic employer who hosts a Christmas Eve party in his warehouse for his employees and others. | Fezziwig is a character who hosts a domestic ball and is praised by his apprentices for making them happy through his kind words and looks.

nodes.name: Three Miss Fezziwigs
nodes.description: The Three Miss Fezziwigs are the daughters of Fezziwig, who are beaming and lovable at the party.

nodes.name: Fiddler
nodes.description: The fiddler is a musician who provides music for the party, tuning his instrument. | The fiddler is a musician playing for the dance, who plays energetically and even resumes playing without rest.

nodes.name: Party Attendees
nodes.description: Various employees and local people attend the Fezziwig Christmas party, including the housemaid, cook, and others.

nodes.name: Dance Event
nodes.description: A social gathering featuring various dances, music, and refreshments like cake and roast.

nodes.name: Sir Roger de Coverley
nodes.description: A dance tune played by the fiddler, prompting the main dance of the evening.

nodes.name: Negus
nodes.description: A warm spiced wine beverage served at the dance event.

nodes.name: Cold Roast
nodes.description: A dish of roasted meat, served cold, at the dance event.

nodes.name: Cold Boiled
nodes.description: A dish of boiled meat, served cold, at the dance event.

nodes.name: Mince-Pies
nodes.description: Sweet pastries filled with mincemeat, served at the dance event.

nodes.name: Dick
nodes.description: Dick is a former apprentice who, along with Scrooge, participates in the ball and later praises Fezziwig.

nodes.name: The Two Apprentices
nodes.description: The two apprentices are former workers at Fezziwig's establishment who pour out their hearts in praise of Fezziwig.

nodes.name: The Domestic Ball
nodes.description: The domestic ball is a festive gathering hosted by Fezziwig and his wife, featuring dancing and ending with Christmas well-wishes.

nodes.name: Young Girl
nodes.description: A fair young girl in mourning dress who confronts Scrooge's former self about how his pursuit of wealth has displaced their relationship. | A beautiful young girl sitting near the fire, who resembles a figure from Scrooge's past, participating in the family's joyful activities.

nodes.name: She
nodes.description: The female character who releases him from their engagement, reflecting on how their relationship has changed.

nodes.name: He
nodes.description: The male character being released from the engagement, feels the justice of the supposition and struggles with it. | He is the deceased man whose belongings are being sold by the women.

nodes.name: The Beautiful Young Girl
nodes.description: A young girl who appears in the new scene, so like the previous girl that Scrooge mistakes her for the same.

nodes.name: Comely Matron
nodes.description: A comely matron sitting opposite her daughter, likely the mother of the young girl, laughing heartily and enjoying the children's play.

nodes.name: Mother
nodes.description: The mother is a comely matron who laughs heartily and enjoys the uproarious activities of the children.

nodes.name: Daughter
nodes.description: The daughter is a young girl who joins in the sports, gets playfully pillaged by the children, and greets her father's return.

nodes.name: Father
nodes.description: The father returns home attended by a man laden with Christmas toys and presents, and is greeted by the children.

nodes.name: Porter
nodes.description: A man laden with Christmas toys and presents who is attacked by the children in a playful manner.

nodes.name: Children
nodes.description: A group of more children than Scrooge can count, each behaving boisterously, engaging in playful attacks and sports.

nodes.name: Winter Fire
nodes.description: A fire in the room where the young girl and others are seated, providing comfort and warmth.

nodes.name: Room
nodes.description: A room that is not very large or handsome, but full of comfort, where the scene takes place.

nodes.name: Christmas Toys
nodes.description: Toys brought by the porter for the children as Christmas presents.

nodes.name: Presents
nodes.description: Presents brought by the porter for the children as Christmas gifts.

nodes.name: Master of the House
nodes.description: The Master of the House is a family man who is happy with his wife and daughter, and is an old friend of Scrooge.

nodes.name: Master's Daughter
nodes.description: The Master's Daughter is a graceful young girl who leans on her father affectionately, symbolizing what Scrooge could have had.

nodes.name: Master's Wife
nodes.description: The Master's Wife is the wife in the family scene, sitting with her daughter and husband.

nodes.name: Scrooge's Office
nodes.description: Scrooge's Office is the place where the Master of the House passes by and sees Scrooge sitting alone. | Scrooge's office is a place that Scrooge observes in the future, finding it occupied by someone else.

nodes.name: Scrooge's Partner
nodes.description: Scrooge's Partner is mentioned as being on the point of death, contributing to Scrooge's isolation.

nodes.name: The Extinguisher-Cap
nodes.description: The Extinguisher-Cap is an object that Scrooge uses to try to cover the Ghost's light.

nodes.name: The Second Spirit
nodes.description: The Second Spirit is the second supernatural messenger sent to Scrooge, expected to appear at One o'clock.

nodes.name: The Bedroom
nodes.description: The Bedroom is where Scrooge finds himself after the encounter with the Ghost and where he prepares for the Second Spirit.

nodes.name: Spontaneous Combustion
nodes.description: Spontaneous combustion is the frightening possibility that Scrooge briefly fears is happening to him, as he is unable to explain the strange light.

nodes.name: Ghostly Light
nodes.description: The ghostly light is a mysterious, alarming illumination that fills Scrooge's room, and which he traces to the adjoining room.

nodes.name: Adjoining Room
nodes.description: The adjoining room is where the ghostly light appears to originate, and it undergoes a surprising transformation into a grove-like space with festive decorations and food.

nodes.name: The Feast
nodes.description: The feast is the collection of food and drink displayed in the transformed room, including turkeys, geese, puddings, and punch, piled up to form a throne.

nodes.name: Plenty's Horn
nodes.description: Plenty's Horn is a symbolic torch held by the Ghost of Christmas Present, resembling the horn of plenty, and used to shed light.

nodes.name: Christmas Morning
nodes.description: Christmas Morning is the setting in which Scrooge and the Ghost find themselves after a magical transition.

nodes.name: City Streets
nodes.description: The city streets are the location on Christmas morning, depicted with snow, mud, and bustling activity.

nodes.name: Snow
nodes.description: Snow covers the rooftops and ground, and is cleared by people and enjoyed by boys who watch it fall.

nodes.name: Great Britain
nodes.description: Great Britain is referenced as the origin of the sooty atoms from chimneys, indicating a broader setting.

nodes.name: Poulterers' Shops
nodes.description: The poulterers' shops are still half open on Christmas morning, part of the bustling holiday scene.

nodes.name: Fruiterers' Shops
nodes.description: The fruiterers' shops are radiant in their glory, displaying produce like chestnuts and onions.

nodes.name: Chestnuts
nodes.description: Chestnuts are displayed in baskets at fruiterers' shops, described as large and pot-bellied.

nodes.name: Spanish Onions
nodes.description: Spanish onions are displayed as ruddy, brown-faced, and broad-girthed at fruiterers' shops. | Spanish onions are a type of vegetable described as ruddy, brown-faced, and broad-girthed, shining like Spanish friars, and winking at the girls from their shelves.

nodes.name: Girls
nodes.description: The girls are passerby who glance demurely at the hung-up mistletoe and are winked at by the Spanish onions.

nodes.name: Mistletoe
nodes.description: Mistletoe is a plant hung up in the shop, glanced at by the girls.

nodes.name: Pears And Apples
nodes.description: Pears and apples are fruits clustered high in blooming pyramids.

nodes.name: Grapes
nodes.description: Grapes are fruits made to dangle from conspicuous hooks to entice passersby.

nodes.name: Filberts
nodes.description: Filberts are nuts, mossy and brown, with a fragrance recalling ancient walks among woods.

nodes.name: Norfolk Biffins
nodes.description: Norfolk Biffins are apples, squab and swarthy, setting off the yellow of oranges and lemons, and entreating to be carried home in paper bags.

nodes.name: Oranges And Lemons
nodes.description: Oranges and lemons are citrus fruits that are yellow and set off by the Norfolk Biffins.

nodes.name: Gold And Silver Fish
nodes.description: Gold and silver fish are fish set forth in a bowl among choice fruits, appearing to know something is going on and gasping in excitement.

nodes.name: The Grocers'
nodes.description: The Grocers' is a shop nearly closed with shutters down, but with glimpses of goods and activities inside.

nodes.name: Scales
nodes.description: Scales are weighing instruments that descend on the counter making a merry sound.

nodes.name: Twine And Roller
nodes.description: Twine and roller are tools used in the grocery that part company briskly.

nodes.name: Canisters
nodes.description: Canisters are containers rattled up and down like juggling tricks.

nodes.name: Tea And Coffee
nodes.description: Tea and coffee are beverages whose blended scents are grateful to the nose.

nodes.name: Raisins
nodes.description: Raisins are dried grapes, plentiful and rare.

nodes.name: Almonds
nodes.description: Almonds are nuts that are extremely white.

nodes.name: Sticks Of Cinnamon
nodes.description: Sticks of cinnamon are long and straight spice sticks.

nodes.name: Other Spices
nodes.description: Other spices are described as delicious.

nodes.name: Candied Fruits
nodes.description: Candied fruits are fruits caked and spotted with molten sugar, making lookers-on feel faint.

nodes.name: Figs
nodes.description: Figs are fruit that are moist and pulpy.

nodes.name: Grocer
nodes.description: The grocer is a shopkeeper whose establishment is described along with the busy customers during Christmas preparations.

nodes.name: Bakers' Shops
nodes.description: The bakers' shops are where people carry their dinners for cooking during Christmas Day.

nodes.name: The Torch
nodes.description: The Spirit's torch is a special implement that sprinkles drops of water and incense on dinners, affecting their recipients' mood.

nodes.name: Christmas Day
nodes.description: Christmas Day is a significant holiday during which the events of the narrative occur. | Christmas Day is the holiday being celebrated by the Cratchit family, during which they enjoy a meal together. | Christmas Day is a holiday on which the Cratchits gather and exchange toasts, despite their feelings about Scrooge. | The holiday that Scrooge learns it is, prompting his joyful transformation.

nodes.name: Incense
nodes.description: Incense is a substance that the Spirit sprinkles from the torch onto dinners.

nodes.name: Water Drops
nodes.description: Water drops from the torch restore good humor to quarreling dinner-carriers.

nodes.name: Master Peter Cratchit
nodes.description: Master Peter Cratchit is the son and heir of Bob Cratchit, who is proudly attired in a shirt with a monstrous collar. | Master Peter Cratchit is one of the Cratchit children, who mashes potatoes and helps fetch the goose.

nodes.name: The Cratchit Dwelling
nodes.description: The Cratchit dwelling is the four-roomed house where Bob Cratchit and his family live, blessed by the Spirit's torch.

nodes.name: The Seventh Day
nodes.description: The Seventh Day refers to a weekly day of rest and dining, which Scrooge suggests is being deprived by the closing of places.

nodes.name: Peter Cratchit
nodes.description: Peter Cratchit is the eldest son of the Cratchit family, who is dressed in his father's shirt-collar and helps with the fire. | Peter Cratchit is the eldest son of the Cratchit family. He is attentive to his father's habits and notes that Bob has been walking slower recently. | Peter Cratchit is the eldest son of the Cratchit family, who is teased by his sisters about his future, and is the subject of a potential job offer. | Peter Cratchit is a character who shakes hands with Bob Cratchit, part of the Cratchit family.

nodes.name: Two Young Cratchits
nodes.description: Two young Cratchit children (boy and girl) are energetic and joyful, running in with news of the goose and teasing Martha. | Two young Cratchits are the younger children who help carry Tiny Tim and set chairs.

nodes.name: The Goose
nodes.description: The goose is a central food item for the Cratchit family's Christmas meal, cooked at the baker's and eagerly anticipated. | The Goose is the main dish of the Christmas dinner, cooked and served by the Cratchit family. | The Goose is the main dish of the Christmas dinner, celebrated for its tenderness, flavour, size, and cheapness.

nodes.name: The Baker's
nodes.description: The baker's is a shop where the Cratchit family's goose is cooked.

nodes.name: The Parks
nodes.description: The fashionable Parks are where Peter Cratchit yearns to show off his new shirt-collar.

nodes.name: Miss Belinda Cratchit
nodes.description: Miss Belinda Cratchit is one of the Cratchit children, who sweetens the apple sauce.

nodes.name: Belinda
nodes.description: Belinda is one of the Cratchit children who assists by changing the plates during the meal.

nodes.name: The Pudding
nodes.description: The Pudding is a dessert prepared by Mrs. Cratchit, served with ignited brandy and Christmas holly, and regarded as a great success. | The pudding is a large dessert made for the Cratchit family's Christmas dinner, considered insufficient by some but no one dared to criticize.

nodes.name: Christmas Dinner
nodes.description: Christmas Dinner is the festive meal shared by the Cratchit family, featuring the goose and pudding.

nodes.name: Cratchit Family
nodes.description: The Cratchit family is the household of Bob Cratchit, including Mrs. Cratchit, Tiny Tim, and other members, gathered for Christmas dinner.

nodes.name: Master Peter
nodes.description: Master Peter is the Cratchits' older son, who is considered for a job situation that would bring in five-and-sixpence weekly.

nodes.name: The Cratchit Family
nodes.description: The Cratchit Family is a family unit that celebrates Christmas together and reacts negatively to the mention of Scrooge. | The Cratchit Family is a close-knit family unit that supports each other through grief, and they share a deep love for Tiny Tim.

nodes.name: Peter
nodes.description: Peter is an individual who reacts to the lord's height by pulling up his collar, suggesting he feels self-conscious or proud. | Peter is a child in the Cratchit family, reading a book to the others.

nodes.name: The Spirit's Torch
nodes.description: The Spirit's torch emits bright sprinklings that make the family look happier at parting.

nodes.name: The Family
nodes.description: The Family is a group of people who are happy, grateful, and contented, despite being poorly dressed and having scanty clothes.

nodes.name: A Lost Child Travelling in the Snow
nodes.description: A Lost Child Travelling in the Snow is a song about a lost child in snow, sung by Tiny Tim.
nodes.id: A Lost Child Travelling in the Snow

nodes.name: The Streets
nodes.description: The Streets are the paths along which Scrooge and the Spirit walk, observing the snowy environs and the lit homes.

nodes.name: Lamplighter
nodes.description: The lamplighter is a person seen on the street who laughs as the Ghost passes, unaware of the Ghost's presence.

nodes.name: Miners
nodes.description: The miners are a group of people who live in the moor and work underground, and they are shown celebrating Christmas with their families.

nodes.name: Old Man
nodes.description: The old man is a miner who sings a Christmas song to his family, and his voice is strong when they join in the chorus.

nodes.name: Moor
nodes.description: The moor is a bleak and desert place with stones and frost, where miners live.

nodes.name: Sea
nodes.description: The sea is a location that the Ghost and Scrooge visit, characterized by thundering water and rocky caverns.

nodes.name: Hut
nodes.description: The hut is a dwelling on the moor where the miners and their families are gathered around a fire.

nodes.name: Lighthouse
nodes.description: A solitary lighthouse built on a reef of sunken rocks, where two men watch the light and celebrate Christmas.

nodes.name: Two Men (Lighthouse)
nodes.description: Two men who watch the lighthouse light, share a can of grog, and wish each other Merry Christmas.

nodes.name: Ship
nodes.description: A ship where the Ghost and Scrooge land, and where every man on board shares Christmas greetings and thoughts.

nodes.name: Scrooge's Niece
nodes.description: Scrooge's niece by marriage is a pretty and spirited woman who laughs heartily and expresses indignation towards Scrooge's attitude. | Scrooge's niece is Fred's wife, who, along with the others, enjoys dinner and interacts warmly with the group. | Scrooge's niece is a female relative of Scrooge who plays the harp skillfully during the family gathering, performing musical pieces that evoke memories for Scrooge. | Scrooge's niece is a woman who joins the games at the party and is seated near Scrooge and the Ghost. | Scrooge's niece by marriage is present at Fred's house and is surprised by Scrooge's arrival.

nodes.name: Assembled Friends
nodes.description: A group of friends gathered with Scrooge's nephew and niece, who laugh heartily in response to the humor.

nodes.name: Laughter
nodes.description: Laughter is described as irresistibly contagious and a noble adjustment in the world.

nodes.name: Topper
nodes.description: Topper is a bachelor who expresses a view on housekeeping and is attracted to one of Scrooge's niece's sisters, likely the plump one. | Topper is a participant in the family gathering, noted for his singing ability in bass, and later for his playful yet deceptive actions during blind man's-buff. | Topper is a guest at the party who engages in the game of blind man's buff and interacts with one of the plump sisters. | Topper is a guest at the party, and appears to be a familiar character who is welcomed.

nodes.name: Plump Sister
nodes.description: The plump sister is one of Scrooge's niece's sisters, who blushes at Topper's comment and attempts to resist laughter with aromatic vinegar. | The plump sister is a relative (likely Fred's sister) who correctly guesses that the animal thought of is Uncle Scrooge. | The plump sister is a guest at the party, and is also warmly welcomed, indicating a larger social gathering.

nodes.name: Plump Sister in the Lace Tucker
nodes.description: The plump sister in the lace tucker is a female guest at the gathering who becomes the focus of Topper's attention during the blind man's-buff game.
nodes.id: Plump Sister in the Lace Tucker

nodes.name: Harp
nodes.description: The harp is a musical instrument played by Scrooge's niece during the family gathering, producing a simple air that is significant to Scrooge.

nodes.name: The Way He Went After That Plump Sister in the Lace Tucker
nodes.description: This is an illustrative caption describing Topper's behavior towards the plump sister during the game of blind man's-buff.
nodes.id: The Way He Went After That Plump Sister in the Lace Tucker

nodes.name: Blind Man's-Buff
nodes.description: Blind man's-buff is a party game played during the gathering, in which Topper targets the plump sister with apparent deception.

nodes.name: The Plump Sister
nodes.description: The plump sister is one of the women at the party who is the target of Topper's attention during the blind man's buff.

nodes.name: Blind Man's Buff
nodes.description: Blind Man's Buff is a party game played at the gathering where one player is blindfolded and tries to catch others.

nodes.name: Yes and No
nodes.description: Yes and No is a game played at the party where one person thinks of something and others ask questions to guess it.

nodes.name: The Party
nodes.description: The party is a festive gathering with games and activities involving the characters. | The party is a celebratory gathering that brought happiness and joy, and is referred to as wonderful.

nodes.name: Uncle Scrooge
nodes.description: Uncle Scrooge is a miserly old man who is the subject of the guessing game; he is later described as becoming gay and light of heart during the vision.

nodes.name: London
nodes.description: London is the city where the animal in the guessing game lives and walks about the streets.

nodes.name: The Animal
nodes.description: The animal in the guessing game is a live, savage creature that growls, grunts, and talks; it is revealed to be Uncle Scrooge.

nodes.name: Mulled Wine
nodes.description: Mulled wine is a drink that Fred raises in a toast to Uncle Scrooge's health.

nodes.name: The Boy
nodes.description: The Boy is one of the two children brought forth by the Ghost, described as yellow, meagre, ragged, and wolfish. | A boy who is compensated by Scrooge, likely for delivering the turkey.

nodes.name: The Girl
nodes.description: The Girl is the other child brought forth by the Ghost, equally wretched and monstrous in appearance. | The girl is a servant in Fred's household who assists Scrooge in finding Fred.

nodes.name: Almshouse
nodes.description: An almshouse is a place of refuge for the poor, referenced as one of the places the spirit leaves his blessing.

nodes.name: Hospital
nodes.description: A hospital is a place for the sick, where the spirit's blessing is also left.

nodes.name: Gaol
nodes.description: A gaol is a jail, another refuge of misery where the spirit bestows his blessing.

nodes.name: Twelfth-Night
nodes.description: Twelfth-Night is a children's party they attend, after which the Ghost's aging is noticed.

nodes.name: Ignorance
nodes.description: Ignorance is a boy child shown to Scrooge, described as Man's child, and is warned against for having Doom written on his brow.

nodes.name: Want
nodes.description: Want is a girl child shown to Scrooge, described as Man's child, representing poverty and need.

nodes.name: The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come
nodes.description: The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come is a solemn Phantom, draped and hooded, that approaches Scrooge after the bell strikes twelve; it points onward but does not speak.
nodes.id: The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come

nodes.name: The City
nodes.description: The City is the urban setting toward which the Spirit points when speaking about the children Ignorance and Want. | The City is the urban setting where the Spirit leads Scrooge, springing up around them and encompassing them as they arrive.

nodes.name: Ghost of the Future
nodes.description: The Ghost of the Future is a silent, spectral figure shrouded in a dusky shroud, pointing ahead to guide Scrooge through the City.

nodes.name: Business Men
nodes.description: Business men are merchants in the City's 'Change, conversing in groups and discussing the death of an unnamed individual.

nodes.name: First Speaker
nodes.description: The first speaker is a man among Scrooge's acquaintances who discusses the deceased man's funeral and money, and later offers to attend the funeral if others do.

nodes.name: Red-Faced Gentleman
nodes.description: A red-faced gentleman with a pendulous excrescence on his nose who inquires about the deceased man's money and jokes about requiring lunch to attend the funeral.

nodes.name: Man with Large Chin
nodes.description: A man with a large chin who responds to the conversation, suggesting the funeral will be cheap and joking about the deceased's will.

nodes.name: Deceased Man
nodes.description: A man who has recently died, whose funeral and money are topics of discussion among the speakers.

nodes.name: First Business Man
nodes.description: A wealthy businessman of great importance who greets the second business man in a brief exchange.

nodes.name: Second Business Man
nodes.description: A wealthy businessman of great importance who responds to the first business man's greeting in a brief conversation.

nodes.name: Jacob
nodes.description: Scrooge's former business partner whose death is referenced in the narrative.

nodes.name: The Future
nodes.description: The temporal realm that the Spirit shows Scrooge, representing the consequences of his actions.

nodes.name: The Porch
nodes.description: A place where Scrooge usually stands but does not see his future self, indicating a change in his life.

nodes.name: The Obscure Quarter
nodes.description: A neglected, foul part of the town previously unknown to Scrooge, marked by crime and poverty.

nodes.name: The Low-Browed Shop
nodes.description: A shop dealing in scrap metal and refuse, where secrets are harbored.

nodes.name: Old Joe
nodes.description: A grey-haired man of nearly seventy years who deals in old iron and other refuse, keeping a shop with a parlour behind a screen of rags. | Old Joe is a purchaser of stolen goods who negotiates prices with the women. | Old Joe is a character involved in distributing gains from the dead man's belongings.

nodes.name: Charwoman
nodes.description: A woman who entered Old Joe's shop first with a heavy bundle, later revealed to be a charwoman.

nodes.name: Laundress
nodes.description: A woman who entered Old Joe's shop second with a heavy bundle, later identified as a laundress.

nodes.name: Undertaker's Man
nodes.description: A man in faded black who entered the shop third, startled upon seeing the women, later identified as an undertaker's man.

nodes.name: Old Joe's Shop
nodes.description: A shop dealing in old iron and refuse, containing heaps of rusty keys, nails, chains, and other junk, with a parlour behind a screen of rags.

nodes.name: Parlour
nodes.description: The space behind the screen of rags in Old Joe's shop where the group gathers.

nodes.name: Rags
nodes.description: Miscellaneous tatters used as a curtain and screen in Old Joe's shop.

nodes.name: Charcoal Stove
nodes.description: A stove made of old bricks used by Old Joe to keep warm in his shop.

nodes.name: The Dead Man
nodes.description: The Dead Man is the deceased individual whose belongings are being plundered, described as a wicked old screw. | The Dead Man is the deceased person whose death is central to the scene, and Scrooge wonders about his life. | The Dead Man is a person who was ill and dying, and whose death brings relief to Caroline and her husband.

nodes.name: The Man in Faded Black
nodes.description: The Man in Faded Black is a participant in the plunder who produces his plunder first.

nodes.name: First Woman
nodes.description: The first woman is one of the women selling items to Old Joe, including bed-curtains and a shirt.

nodes.name: The Corpse
nodes.description: The corpse is the dead man whose body is displayed on a bed, and whose life story is the focus of the scene.

nodes.name: The Phantom
nodes.description: The Phantom is a ghostly figure guiding Scrooge through the visions, pointing to the corpse's head.

nodes.name: The Lamp
nodes.description: A lamp providing light in the scene with the corpse, used by the old man.

nodes.name: Death
nodes.description: Death is personified as a force with dominion over the scene, but powerless over the good deeds of the dead.

nodes.name: Caroline's Husband
nodes.description: Caroline's Husband is a young man who brings the news of the Dead Man's death, showing a mix of relief and shame. | Caroline's husband informs her of the man's death and discusses their debt.

nodes.name: The Mother
nodes.description: The Mother is Caroline, who is anxious waiting for her husband and finds hope after the bad news.

nodes.name: The Cat
nodes.description: A cat is present in the dark, empty house, tearing at the door, contributing to the fearful atmosphere.

nodes.name: The Rats
nodes.description: Rats are gnawing beneath the hearthstone in the house, adding to the sense of decay and fear.

nodes.name: The Dark Empty House
nodes.description: A house where the Dead Man lies, described as dark and empty, with no one to mourn him.

nodes.name: The Lesson
nodes.description: The Lesson refers to the moral insight Scrooge gains from the death scene, which he vows not to forget.

nodes.name: Half-Drunken Woman
nodes.description: Half-Drunken Woman is a woman who informed Caroline's husband about the dead man's critical condition.

nodes.name: Cratchit's Wife
nodes.description: Cratchit's Wife is the mother of the Cratchit children, engaged in sewing and caring for the family.

nodes.name: The Children
nodes.description: The Children are the Cratchit children, who are quiet and seated around the fire.

nodes.name: The Debt
nodes.description: The Debt is a financial obligation owed by Caroline and her husband, which they plan to repay.

nodes.name: The Formerly Dark Chamber
nodes.description: The Formerly Dark Chamber is a place Scrooge was shown earlier, which he references.

nodes.name: Mr. Scrooge's Nephew
nodes.description: Mr. Scrooge's nephew is a kind and generous gentleman who meets Bob in the street, shows concern for his distress, and offers his help.

nodes.name: Churchyard
nodes.description: The churchyard is a graveyard where Scrooge is shown a grave, representing his potential future.

nodes.name: The Grave
nodes.description: The grave is a specific burial site in the churchyard that the Ghost points to, symbolizing Scrooge's potential death.

nodes.name: Ghost Of Christmas Present
nodes.description: The Ghost of Christmas Present is a spirit that sat in the corner of Scrooge's room during the visitation.

nodes.name: Christmas Time
nodes.description: Christmas Time is a holiday season that Scrooge praises and celebrates with joy and good intentions.

nodes.name: Bed Curtains
nodes.description: The bed curtains are physical objects in Scrooge's room that Scrooge holds and inspects, affirming they were not torn down.

nodes.name: The Gruel Saucepan
nodes.description: The gruel saucepan is a cooking vessel that Scrooge identifies in his room, part of his tangible connection to the events of the night.

nodes.name: The Door
nodes.description: The door is a physical feature in Scrooge's room through which the Ghost of Jacob Marley entered.

nodes.name: The Window
nodes.description: The window is an opening in Scrooge's room from which he saw wandering Spirits, and later opens to view the outside.

nodes.name: Boy
nodes.description: A boy in Sunday clothes who Scrooge sends to buy the turkey.

nodes.name: The Prize Turkey
nodes.description: The big prize turkey that Scrooge decides to buy and send to Bob Cratchit's family.

nodes.name: The Spirits
nodes.description: Supernatural beings who visited Scrooge and transformed him in one night.

nodes.name: The Knocker
nodes.description: The door knocker on Scrooge's door that he now appreciates.

nodes.name: The Turkey
nodes.description: A large turkey that Scrooge buys and sends to Camden Town, symbolizing his generosity.

nodes.name: The Portly Gentleman
nodes.description: A gentleman who visited Scrooge's counting-house the previous day and is approached by Scrooge for an apology.

nodes.name: Camden Town
nodes.description: A location in London where Scrooge sends the turkey.

nodes.name: The Gentleman
nodes.description: The gentleman is a collector for charity who is astonished by Scrooge's generous donation.

nodes.name: Dinner
nodes.description: Dinner is a specific meal that Fred arrives for, highlighting the social context of the story.

nodes.name: The Tank
nodes.description: The tank is the workspace area where Bob Cratchit works, and it is where Scrooge confronts him.

nodes.name: The Office
nodes.description: The office is the workplace where Scrooge and Bob Cratchit interact, significant to the plot.

nodes.name: Total-Abstinence Principle
nodes.description: The Total-Abstinence Principle is a principle that Scrooge lived upon after his transformation.

The Spirit blesses Bob Cratchit's dwelling with the sprinklings of his torch.

Bob Cratchit lives in the four-roomed house known as the Cratchit dwelling.
Master Peter Cratchit is Bob's son and heir, who wears Bob's shirt-collar.

Bob Cratchit is the husband of Mrs. Cratchit. | Bob and Mrs. Cratchit share a close bond, supporting each other through the loss of Tiny Tim. | Bob and Mrs. Cratchit are married and share affection, often working together around the fire. | Mrs. Cratchit kisses Bob Cratchit in a moment of family happiness.
Bob Cratchit is initially disappointed that Martha is not coming, then joyfully embraces her when she appears. | Bob Cratchit hugs Martha after she comes out from behind the closet door.
Bob Cratchit praised the goose as the best ever cooked.
Bob Cratchit regarded the pudding as the greatest success achieved by Mrs. Cratchit since their marriage.
Bob Cratchit leads the family gathering around the hearth and proposes a Christmas toast.
Bob Cratchit tells the family about a job situation for Master Peter that would bring in five-and-sixpence weekly.
Bob expresses hope that Peter will receive a better situation through the kindness of Mr. Scrooge's nephew.
Bob appreciates the kindness of Mr. Scrooge's nephew, who offered help and gave his card.
Bob Cratchit works in the tank, which is his designated space in the office.
Mrs. Cratchit asks how Tiny Tim behaved, showing her concern for him. | Mrs. Cratchit recalls how Bob used to walk with Tiny Tim on his shoulder, expressing her sadness over Tiny Tim's absence.
The two young Cratchits hustle Tiny Tim to the wash-house and later set chairs for him.
Tiny Tim hopes that people remember on Christmas Day the miracle of healing, reflecting on his own condition.
Tiny Tim expressed excitement and joy during the serving of the goose.

The Ghost predicts that Tiny Tim will die if the future remains unaltered.

Cratchit's wife reacts emotionally to the mention of Tiny Tim's illness or death.

The entire Cratchit family mourns the loss of Tiny Tim and remembers him with love and sorrow.

The Ghost of Christmas Present visits Scrooge and offers to guide him and teach him lessons.
The Ghost of Christmas Present holds a torch shaped like Plenty's Horn to spread light.

Mrs. Cratchit expresses admiration for Mr. Scrooge's nephew, calling him a good soul.
Martha Cratchit, as an apprentice, shares details of her work and her plans to rest on the holiday.

Scrooge dismisses Christmas as a time for paying bills without money and wishes to punish those who celebrate it. | Scrooge dismisses Christmas, stating he does not make merry at Christmas and cannot afford to make idle people merry. | Scrooge is implied to hold a negative view of Christmas, calling it a humbug. | Christmas is a pivotal theme that influences Scrooge's transformation from miserly to generous.
Mr. Marley was Scrooge's business partner who died seven years ago.
The portly gentlemen approach Scrooge for charitable donations, referencing his firm's name.
Scrooge is the surviving partner of the firm Scrooge and Marley's.
Scrooge interacts with the Gentleman, who requests a donation for the poor, but Scrooge refuses to give anything.
Scrooge asks about prisons, suggesting they are an existing means of supporting the poor.
Scrooge asks if the Union workhouses are still in operation, indicating his reliance on such institutions.
Scrooge mentions the Treadmill as a symbol of the penal system in operation.
Scrooge references the Poor Law as an existing mechanism for dealing with the poor.
The Gentlemen withdraw after failing to persuade Scrooge, who resumes his work.
The carol singer attempts to sing a Christmas carol at Scrooge's keyhole.
Scrooge owns and operates the counting-house, where he works and employs the clerk.
Scrooge seizes the ruler to frighten away the carol singer.
Scrooge's aggressive reaction with the ruler frightens the singer away.
Scrooge takes his melancholy dinner at the tavern.
Scrooge lives in the chambers that once belonged to his deceased partner.
Scrooge grudgingly gives the clerk the day off for Christmas Eve.

Scrooge lives in the house and knows its every stone; he has resided there for his entire residence in the City of London. | Scrooge secures his house, checks his rooms, and locks himself in, demonstrating caution within his own home.
Scrooge sees the door knocker transform into Marley's face while he is about to enter the house.
Scrooge observes the bell begin to swing and ring, causing him astonishment and inexplicable dread.
Scrooge hears the clanking of a heavy chain below, associating it with ghosts dragging chains.

Scrooge confronts the Ghost with doubt and tries to dismiss it as a hallucination caused by indigestion. | The Ghost challenges Scrooge's skepticism and reveals its frightening nature to persuade him of its reality. | The Ghost draws aside Scrooge's bed curtains and appears face to face with him, causing Scrooge to start up in a half-recumbent attitude. | The Ghost leads Scrooge to revisit his past and points out significant scenes, including his lonely school days. | Scrooge observes the Ghost and glances anxiously towards the door in its presence. | Scrooge is accompanied by the Ghost and is reminded of his past through its visions. | The Ghost forces Scrooge to observe the next scene despite Scrooge's pleas to stop. | Scrooge attempts to extinguish the Ghost's light using the extinguisher-cap, but the light remains unbroken. | Scrooge follows the Ghost's instruction to touch its robe, initiating the vision. | The Ghost commands Scrooge to touch its robe, leading to a magical transition to Christmas morning. | The Ghost shows Scrooge the Cratchit family and reveals the potential death of Tiny Tim if the future remains unchanged. | Scrooge pleads with the Ghost to spare Tiny Tim's life. | The Ghost rebukes Scrooge for his judgments and leads him to observe the Cratchit family. | Scrooge and the Ghost are together at the party, with the Ghost observing Scrooge's enjoyment. | Scrooge interacts with the Ghost, who teaches him precepts and shows him the two children. | Scrooge is guided and confronted by The Ghost in a fearful place, discussing the dead man. | The Ghost conducts Scrooge to various scenes, including the Cratchit house. | The Ghost shows Scrooge his grave and future, prompting Scrooge's plea for change.

edges.target: The Old Ghost in a White Waistcoat
edges.description: Scrooge recognizes the old ghost and observes its sorrow over its inability to help others.
Scrooge's glimpse of the Invisible World contributes to his emotional exhaustion and need for rest.
Scrooge listens to the church bell striking the hours, which indicates the time and leads to his astonishment.
Scrooge listens to the hour bell and counts the quarters and the hour.

Scrooge is being led by the Spirit through a past experience, who provides support and ensures Scrooge can traverse realms. | Scrooge interacts with the Spirit, asking questions about the torch and the Spirit's actions.

Scrooge recalls and recognizes the market-town and its features (bridge, church, river) as part of his past.
Scrooge sees and names the boys he knew in his youth, feeling unexpected joy and gladness at their sight.
Scrooge revisits the school where he was left alone as a child, and weeps at the memory.
Scrooge recalls Ali Baba appearing at the window during a past Christmas, expressing fondness for the character.
Scrooge mentions Valentine as part of the story characters he remembers from his past.
Scrooge mentions Orson as Valentine's wild brother in the stories he recalls.
Scrooge recalls the Parrot from the story and its appearance.
Scrooge recalls Friday running to the creek as part of the story.

Scrooge interacts with the Spirit, who asks about Scrooge's sadness and offers to show another Christmas. | The Spirit and Scrooge engage in a dialogue about the closing of places on the Seventh Day. | Scrooge and the Spirit walk together along the streets, with the Spirit guiding the experience. | Scrooge looks to the Spirit for explanations of the conversations and scenes he is shown. | The Spirit accompanies Scrooge and directs his attention to events in the future.

Scrooge is at the school when Fan arrives to take him home.

Scrooge remembers Fezziwig positively, recognizing the value of his kindness and generosity.

She is part of Scrooge's memory that he is forced to witness, causing him emotional distress.

Scrooge's partner lies on the point of death, and Scrooge is left alone, highlighting his isolation.
Scrooge seizes and presses the extinguisher-cap down on the Ghost, but fails to hide the light.
Scrooge prepares to meet the Second Spirit, which is sent to him through Jacob Marley's intervention.

Scrooge traces the source of the ghostly light to the adjoining room and decides to enter it.
Scrooge briefly fears he might be undergoing spontaneous combustion as an explanation for the light.
Scrooge and the Ghost stand in the city streets on Christmas morning after the magical transition.
Scrooge discusses the Seventh Day with the Spirit, expressing concern about depriving people of dining.
Scrooge is viewed negatively by the Cratchit family, who see him as an ogre and his name casts a shadow on their party.
Scrooge is taken to the moor by the Ghost and asks what place it is.
Scrooge is taken to the sea, which horrifies him.

Scrooge joins in the games and is interested in the activities at the party.
Scrooge attends a Twelfth-Night party with the Ghost and observes the Ghost's aging.
Scrooge asks about the children's refuge, indicating concern for Ignorance and Want.

Scrooge follows the Spirit through the City, observing the merchants and their activities.

Scrooge knows the businessmen and has always sought their esteem strictly in a business point of view.
Jacob was Scrooge's old partner whose death is mentioned, though not the focus of the current lesson.
Scrooge's usual corner at the Porch is occupied by another man, indicating his intended change of life.
Scrooge is taken to an unfamiliar, squalid part of town, highlighting the consequences of neglect.
Scrooge watches Old Joe's dealings and feels detestation.
Scrooge views the first woman with disgust as she sells the stolen goods.
Scrooge is guided by the Phantom through visions of the dead man's fate.

Scrooge praises Christmas Time, expressing joy and good intentions.
Scrooge remembers that the Ghost of Christmas Present sat in the corner of the room.
Scrooge holds the bed curtains and affirms they are not torn down, indicating relief about his reality.
Scrooge sees wandering Spirits from the window and later opens it to view the bright outside.
Scrooge buys the big prize turkey to send to Bob Cratchit's family.
Scrooge instructs the Boy to buy the turkey and bring it back.
Scrooge acknowledges the Spirits' role in his change and that they achieved it in one night.
Scrooge rejoices that it is Christmas Day and that he hasn't missed it.
Scrooge professes love for the knocker, reflecting his changed attitude.
Scrooge buys a turkey and sends it to Camden Town, showing his generosity.
Scrooge recompenses the boy for his services likely related to the turkey delivery.
Scrooge apologizes to the gentleman and asks for his pardon.
Scrooge sends the turkey to Camden Town.
Scrooge gives a generous donation to the gentleman's charity, including back-payments.
Scrooge is at the office early to confront Bob, indicating his role as an employer.

Old Joe and the woman are involved in dividing the dead man's money.

Fred is Scrooge's nephew who proposes a toast to him despite Scrooge's previous rejection.
The plump sister correctly guesses that the animal is Uncle Scrooge, addressing Fred in her excitement.
Fred questions the animal about its characteristics, driving the guessing game.
Fred uses a glass of mulled wine to propose a toast to Uncle Scrooge.
The firm Scrooge and Marley retains Marley's name, linking Marley to the business even after his death.
Marley's Ghost is the apparition of Marley, appearing with his characteristic look and ghostly spectacles.
The door knocker temporarily transforms into the face of Marley's ghost before reverting back.
Marley's Ghost is bound by the chain, representing the weight of his past deeds.
Marley's Ghost sits down opposite the fireplace, establishing a setting for the conversation with Scrooge.

The clerk's fire is very small, resembling a single coal, and is insufficient to keep him warm.
The clerk is employed at Scrooge's counting-house and works there.
Christmas Eve is the reason the clerk is given a day off and celebrates by sliding on Cornhill.

The Spirit looks at the nephew with approving affability. | The Spirit stands by Scrooge's side looking at Scrooge's nephew with approving affability.

Scrooge's nephew participates in the party games, including thinking of an animal in Yes and No.

The Gentleman chooses Christmas as the time for fundraising because Want is keenly felt.
The Ghost spreads Christmas spirit and mirth.
The Gentleman and his colleague are raising a fund to provide the Poor with meat, drink, and warmth.
The ancient tower becomes invisible in the fog, with its bell sounding from the clouds.
The Lord Mayor gives orders from the Mansion House, his stronghold.
The little tailor was fined by the Lord Mayor for being drunk and bloodthirsty.
The ragged men and boys gather around a fire to warm themselves against the intense cold.
The singer sings a Christmas carol at Scrooge's keyhole.
In life, Marley's spirit never roved beyond the counting-house, indicating his limited and selfish focus.
The Genius of the Weather sits in mournful meditation on the threshold of the house, contributing to the dreary atmosphere.
Marley is fettered by a chain that he forged in life, symbolizing his sins and missed opportunities.
The ghost carries a chain that represents the burdens of his past actions and serves as a visual metaphor for his remorse.
The Dutch Merchant built the old fireplace where the low fire burns.
Peter Cratchit blows the fire to cook the potatoes.
The Ghost is revealed to be the spirit of Jacob Marley, Scrooge's former business partner.
The ghost asserts that the common welfare should be everyone's business, contrasting with his own past neglect.
The Second Spirit was despatched to Scrooge through Jacob Marley's intervention.
The Ghost joins the phantoms in their mournful dirge before leaving.
The Ghost points out Fezziwig's actions and questions the extent of his generosity.
The Ghost observes the party and Scrooge's participation in it.
The Ghost shows Scrooge various scenes of life, contributing to his internal change.
The Ghost brings forth the boy from under its robe and presents him to Scrooge.
The Ghost brings forth the girl from under its robe and presents her to Scrooge.
The Ghost leaves his blessing in almshouses.
The Ghost leaves his blessing in hospitals.
The Ghost leaves his blessing in gaols.
The Ghost points to the Dead Man's head, indicating the significance of his death.
Scrooge refers to the dark chamber he was shown earlier, expressing it will be ever present.
The concept of a Christian spirit working kindly aligns with the ideal of caring for mankind's welfare.
The Spirit states that the boys are but shadows of things that have been, and they have no consciousness of Scrooge and the Spirit.
The Spirit stands with Scrooge in a baker's doorway and sprinkles incense on dinners as bearers pass.
The Spirit uses the torch to sprinkle drops of water and incense on dinners.
The Spirit sheds water drops from the torch on quarreling dinner-carriers, restoring their good humor.
The Spirit sprinkles incense on dinners from the torch.
The Spirit and his actions are associated with the celebration of Christmas Day.
Boys ride ponies or are carried in gigs and carts driven by farmers, traveling toward the market-town.
The young Scrooge is a solitary child, neglected by friends, left at the school during the holidays.
The young Scrooge is reading about Ali Baba, seeing him as a vivid and comforting figure.
The Genii turned the Sultan's Groom upside down, as recalled by Scrooge.
The Sultan's Groom was married to the Princess, an event Scrooge mentions.
Robin Crusoe called the Parrot 'Poor Robin Crusoe' when he returned home.
The Spirit uses its torch to create bright sprinklings that make the family appear happier at parting.
The Spirit shows Scrooge the boy Ignorance and warns that he is dangerous because Doom is written on his brow.
The Spirit shows Scrooge the girl Want as another child clinging to the Spirit.
The Spirit reveals scenes from the future to Scrooge for his moral improvement.
The schoolmaster brings Scrooge and Fan to the parlour and serves them wine and cake.
Master Scrooge bids the schoolmaster goodbye as he leaves the school in a chaise.
The Ghost accompanies Master Scrooge and shows him scenes from his past, including his departure from school.
Master Scrooge was apprenticed at the warehouse, as he recognizes when the Ghost brings him there.
Master Scrooge recognizes Old Fezziwig as his former employer and expresses excitement at seeing him alive again.
The schoolmaster produces a decanter of curiously light wine and serves it to the young people.
The schoolmaster produces a block of curiously heavy cake and serves it to the young people.
The Ghost takes Scrooge to see Old Fezziwig at his warehouse, invoking a memory of Scrooge's apprenticeship.
The lamplighter laughs as the Ghost passes, though he does not know the Ghost is there.
The Ghost indicates that the miners know him, and later shows them to Scrooge.
Old Fezziwig organized and led the dance event, clapping hands to stop dances and encouraging participants.
Fezziwig's warehouse is the venue for the Christmas Eve party, transformed into a ballroom.
The fiddler sets up in the warehouse and provides music for the party.
Fezziwig is the father of the Three Miss Fezziwigs, who are present at the party.
Fezziwig hosts the Christmas Eve party and welcomes all the attendees into his warehouse.

Cold Boiled was a dish provided at the dance event.
Mince-pies were a dessert at the dance event.
The apprentices attend the domestic ball hosted by Fezziwig and his wife.

The first woman took items from the deceased man's body and is now selling them.
The mother laughs heartily with her daughter, enjoying the children's activities.
The daughter greets her father when he comes home.
The children pillage the daughter's belongings and engage in rough play with her.

The Christmas toys are given to the children as presents.

Snow covers the streets and rooftops, contributing to the festive atmosphere.

Spanish onions are displayed at the fruiterers' shops.

Girls glance demurely at the hung-up mistletoe.
Grapes were made by shopkeepers to dangle from conspicuous hooks to entice passersby.
Norfolk Biffins set off the yellow of the oranges and lemons.
The blended scents of tea and coffee are grateful to the nose in the Grocers'.
Candied fruits are so caked and spotted with molten sugar that they make the coldest lookers-on feel faint.
The grocer's shop is mentioned alongside the bakers' shops in the description of Christmas shopping.

Master Peter helps fetch the goose and prepares it by mashing potatoes.
Peter Cratchit yearns to show his new shirt-collar in the fashionable Parks.
Peter might benefit from a better situation due to the kindness of Mr. Scrooge's nephew.
The young Cratchits smell the goose at the baker's and recognize it as their own.
The goose is cooked at the baker's.
Miss Belinda helps with the meal by sweetening the apple sauce.

The Christmas dinner was the festive meal shared by the Cratchit family.

Peter reads a book to the gathered children.

The two men watch the lighthouse light and make a fire to shed brightness on the sea.
Every man on the ship shares Christmas thoughts and greetings, remembering those at a distance.

Scrooge's niece participates in the games and is seated near Scrooge and the Ghost.
Topper has his eye on the plump sister, causing her to blush when he mentions his bachelor status.
